newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission points to progress on US veterinary accord.
newsitem.headline: Commission points to progress on US veterinary accord.

text.p: Progress was being made with the United States on veterinary and phytosanitary equivalency agreements but a lot of work remained to be done to achieve the end-year deadline, European Commission officials said.

The agreement, which involves mutual recognition of animal and plant health standards, covers trade in live animals, fresh and processed meat, pet food, plants and plant products worth up to $5.0 billion annually.
"We are working on a consolidated text," a senior Commission agriculture source said after two days of what he described as "cordial" talks with USDA officials.
"The process seems to be back on track," the source said, noting that Washington was now making a considerable effort to get an agreement.
On the EU side, there were two major obstacles.
Firstly, Brussels is insisting that Washington sign up to agreements with the EU and not to the individual member states.
Secondly, Brussels wants Washington to accept the principle of "regionalisation."
The provision allows for the placing of trade curbs to deal with animal and plant diseases on a regional basis instead of on the whole EU.
Commission sources point out that the EU accepted regional measures implemented by Washington to contain and curb the karnal bundt wheat fungus.

"We could have said no more U.S. wheat until the disease was totally eradicated," one source said, noting Washington's refusal to give Spain a clean bill of health until African Swine Fever was completely eliminated in that country.
On the U.S. side, Washington is concerned about the extension of national standards into common EU standards, especially in the sensitive livestock trade.
EU sources noted that similar animal and plant health agreements with New Zealand were at an advanced stage and draft texts were being sent to member states for scrutiny.
